analysis.headline: Passed the House 224-194 on February 6, 2020, but the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee never acted on it and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Protecting the Right to Organize (PRO) Act would have rewritten the National Labor Relations Act to make it easier for workers to form unions and bargain collectively. It would have redefined who counts as an employee, imposed real money penalties on employers who fire or retaliate against workers for organizing, let workers sue their employers directly, banned forced arbitration agreements that block workers from joining class actions, and overridden state 'right-to-work' laws so union contracts could require fees from all workers a union represents.
analysis.who_benefits: Private-sector workers — especially those in industries where union organizing is difficult today, such as gig platforms, fast food, and warehouses — plus existing union members who would get stronger remedies when employers violate labor law. The CRS summary states the bill broadens who counts as an employee under federal labor law [S4], which would extend collective-bargaining protections to many workers currently classified as independent contractors [S5].

how_it_helps.text: It would make it an unfair labor practice for an employer to permanently replace or discriminate against workers who participate in strikes, and to require or coerce employees to attend meetings designed to discourage union membership [S2][S4].

It would impose civil penalties of up to $50,000 per violation (up to $100,000 for repeat offenders) on employers who commit unfair labor practices, plus double the actual damages (back pay and consequential damages) for fired workers, and allow punitive damages — current law has essentially no monetary penalties for these violations [S5][S4].
It would create a private right of action, letting workers sue employers in federal court for interfering with their right to organize, with attorney's fees available to prevailing workers [S4][S5].
It would prohibit employers from requiring employees to sign agreements waiving their right to join class or collective lawsuits over workplace disputes, voiding such agreements [S4][S5].

It would tighten the definitions of 'employee,' 'supervisor,' and 'employer' (including a joint-employer standard) so that workers cannot be classified out of labor-law protections, and would apply an ABC test making a worker an employee unless the employer meets three conditions showing genuine independence [S3][S2][S5].

It would speed up union representation elections — setting deadlines for hearings and requiring elections within 20 business days — prohibit employers from participating as parties in representation proceedings, require employers to hand over voter contact lists to the union, and require an employer to bargain once a union wins a majority of votes cast [S4][S5].

It would allow first contracts for newly certified unions to be settled by binding arbitration if mediation fails, and permit 'fair share' fees in union contracts regardless of state right-to-work laws [S4][S5].
It would add whistleblower protections covering employees who report labor-law violations and add new remedies including reinstatement, back pay with interest, and compensatory damages [S4][S5].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, and most directly companies that spend heavily opposing unionization: they would face civil penalties up to $50,000 per violation, doubled liquidated and punitive damages in lawsuits, director and officer liability, mandatory arbitration of first contracts, and reporting requirements for 'persuader' arrangements with anti-union consultants [S5][S4]. Businesses using independent contractors, including gig-economy platforms, would bear reclassification costs under the new employee definition [S5]. Companies in the 27 or so right-to-work states would lose the ability to run open-shop workplaces under union contracts [S5].

drawbacks.text: The bill would override state right-to-work laws: collective-bargaining agreements could require all employees in a bargaining unit to pay fees to the union 'notwithstanding any State or Territorial law' [S4][S5]. Workers who choose not to join a union would still have to pay under such contracts, which critics view as forcing financial support for an organization they declined to join.

It would prohibit employers from participating in any NLRB representation proceedings and from communicating their position during them [S4], removing the employer's voice from the election process entirely — a significant shift from the current adversarial-but-balanced election model.

It would require binding tripartite arbitration to settle first contracts if mediation fails after 90 days, with the award binding for two years [S5]. Opponents argue this substitutes government-appointed arbitrators' terms for negotiated agreements.

It would permit secondary strikes — unions encouraging members to honor strikes at companies they do not have a contract with — and repeal employers' right to sue over such strikes [S4][S5], which business groups argue exposes neutral third-party businesses to labor disputes they are not party to.

The ABC-test employee definition would classify many currently independent workers as employees [S5], which could change how gig and freelance workers structure their work, a cost supporters of the bill acknowledge comes with extending bargaining protections.

The bill also permits labor organizations to participate in strikes initiated by other unions' employees and would remove current limits on courts issuing temporary injunctions against employers [S4], changes that expand union leverage in disputes beyond individual workplaces.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the bill addressed a well-documented structural problem: federal labor law currently carries almost no monetary penalty for employers who fire or retaliate against organizers, so violations can be cheaper than compliance. The PRO Act would have changed that calculus with real penalties, a private right of action, faster elections, and arbitration of first contracts. The serious counterweights are real: overriding state right-to-work laws compels fees from non-union workers under fair-share contracts, excluding employers from representation elections and permitting secondary strikes shift leverage sharply toward unions, and the independent-contractor test would force reclassification with uncertain effects on gig workers who value flexibility. Weighing it honestly: the bill substantially strengthened worker bargaining rights at a substantial cost to employer discretion, and reasonable people disagree about where that balance should sit; the procedural history, however, is not a judgment on those merits — the Senate never voted on the bill at all.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 224-194, but the Senate referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on February 10, 2020, and it never received a Senate vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced May 2, 2019, and referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor [S1][S7].
The committee ordered the bill reported as amended by a vote of 26-21 on September 25, 2019, and formally reported it on December 16, 2019 [S7].
A motion to recommit with instructions failed 195-223 on February 6, 2020, with 192 Republicans voting yes and no Republicans voting no [S8][S7].
The House passed the bill 224-194 on February 6, 2020: 219 Democrats and 5 Republicans voted yes, while 186 Republicans, 7 Democrats, and 1 Independent voted no [S9][S7].

The Senate received the bill on February 10, 2020, and read it twice before referring it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions; no further action was taken for the remainder of the 116th Congress [S7][S5].

key_actors.name: Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott
key_actors.role: U.S. Representative (D-VA); bill sponsor and Chairman of the House Committee on Education and Labor
key_actors.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 2, 2019 and shepherded it through his committee, which ordered it reported as amended 26-21 and reported it on December 16, 2019 [S1][S7].

key_actors.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
key_actors.role: Committee of jurisdiction in the House
key_actors.what_they_did: Held a markup on September 25, 2019, ordered the bill reported as amended by a 26-21 vote, and reported it with House Report 116-347 [S7].

key_actors.name: House Committee on Rules
key_actors.role: House committee that sets floor debate terms
key_actors.what_they_did: Reported H. Res. 833 on February 5, 2020, providing a structured rule for one hour of debate on H.R. 2474 [S7].

key_actors.name: House members voting on passage
key_actors.what_they_did: Passed the bill 224-194 on February 6, 2020 (Roll no. 50), with near-unanimous Democratic support, 5 Republican votes in favor, and 7 Democrats opposed [S9][S7].

key_actors.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
key_actors.role: Committee of jurisdiction in the Senate
key_actors.what_they_did: Received the bill on February 10, 2020 after House passage; the committee took no recorded action, and the Senate never voted on the bill before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S7][S5][S1].
